headline: Mont Blanc Is a Little Shorter This Year

sentences.text: Mont Blanc is the highest mountain in Western Europe.
It is in France, near the border with Italy.
This year, the top of the mountain is 4,807 meters high.
Last year it was more than one meter higher.
The snow on top changes with the weather every year.
Mont Blanc, the highest mountain in Western Europe, has become a little shorter.
New measurements show the peak is now 4,807 meters above sea level.
That is more than one meter lower than the result from last year.
The rock does not move, but the snow and ice on top change every year.
Warm summers and strong winds can take away some of the snow.
Experts say the height will probably go up again in a colder year.
Mont Blanc, often called the roof of Europe, has lost more than a meter of height in a single year.
A new survey puts the summit of the French mountain at 4,807 meters above sea level.
The peak is covered by a thick cap of snow and ice, and the rock below is much lower.
Because the cap grows and shrinks with the weather, the official height changes from year to year.
Surveyors have measured the mountain regularly for years to track these changes.
They say a hot summer, strong winds and less snowfall can all make the summit lower.
The next measurement may show the mountain growing again if the coming winter is snowy.
Mont Blanc, the highest peak in Western Europe, is more than a meter shorter than it was a year ago, according to a new survey.
The summit of the French mountain now stands at 4,807 meters above sea level.
The figure refers to the top of the permanent snow and ice cap rather than the rock beneath it, which sits considerably lower.
Because that cap is shaped by snowfall, wind and summer temperatures, the recorded height rises and falls from one year to the next.
Surveyors have been tracking the summit for years, and the results are followed closely by climbers and climate researchers alike.
The latest drop is being linked to changing conditions in the Alps, including warmer summers and shifting wind patterns.
Experts caution that a single year's figure is not a trend in itself, and the mountain could regain height after a snowy winter.
Even so, the measurements offer a vivid snapshot of how quickly conditions at high altitude can change.
Mont Blanc, the celebrated roof of Europe, has shed more than a meter of height in the space of a year, a new survey has found.
The summit of the French peak, which straddles the border with Italy, now stands at 4,807 meters above sea level.
That figure describes the crest of the permanent snow and ice cap rather than the bedrock, which lies some way beneath it.
Since the cap is sculpted by snowfall, wind and summer temperatures, the mountain's official height fluctuates from one survey to the next.
Teams of surveyors have measured the summit at regular intervals for years, and their findings are scrutinized by mountaineers and climate scientists alike.
This year's decline has been attributed to shifting Alpine conditions, including warmer summers that thin the snowpack and winds that scour the ridge.
Specialists are careful to point out that one measurement does not amount to a trend, and that a generous winter could restore the lost meter.
Nevertheless, the figures provide a striking illustration of how swiftly the high-altitude environment is being reshaped.
